summary: Networks both help reduce humanity's environmental footprint and add to it. This informational document surveys challenges and opportunities for managing networks in more energy-efficient, sustainable ways. It frames the problems for further work rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers and cables use a lot of electricity. This paper asks how we can run the internet so it wastes less power and is kinder to the planet.

questions: how to make networks more sustainable
subtitle: Research challenges and opportunities for managing networks to reduce energy consumption and environmental impact.

tldr.problem: Networks consume significant energy and contribute to climate change through greenhouse gas emissions. While networks enable applications that reduce environmental impact, networking technology itself must become more energy-efficient and sustainable to meet climate goals.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC identifies challenges and opportunities across four levels: equipment-level improvements to hardware efficiency and instrumentation; protocol-level optimizations for reduced data transmission and energy-aware operations; network-level optimization through carbon-aware routing and resource management; and architecture-level shifts like edge computing that reduce long-distance transmission.
tldr.outcome: The document provides a research roadmap for making networking technology greener without losing utility. It emphasizes network management's outsized role in achieving sustainability through optimized resource usage, energy-aware routing, and automated control loops for continuous adaptation.

today: RFC 9845 is an IRTF Informational RFC published in October 2025. It represents the consensus of the Network Management Research Group. The document reflects ongoing work as of 2024-2025 on green metrics standardization and YANG data models for power measurement. It is not an IETF standard but rather a research roadmap. Network operators including Telefónica have demonstrated that significant efficiency gains are achievable through systematic management and optimization. The document serves as a comprehensive guide for researchers, network operators, and standards bodies seeking to reduce networking's environmental footprint.

sections.title: Motivation and Scope
sections.content:
Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is critical for addressing climate change. Networks help reduce emissions by enabling teleconferencing and remote work instead of travel, and by powering IoT applications that optimize agriculture, buildings, and smart cities. However, networks themselves consume significant energy and thus contribute substantially to emissions.

Green networking refers to technology that improves networking sustainability by lowering greenhouse gas emissions (carbon footprint), increasing energy efficiency, and enabling greater use of renewable energy sources. The goal is not merely to reduce energy consumption but to achieve net-zero emissions through a holistic approach considering energy mix, manufacturing impacts, cooling efficiency, and lifecycle factors.

The RFC approaches the problem at four technical levels: equipment (hardware and instrumentation), protocols (transmission efficiency and enablement of management), networks (routing, optimization, and resource management), and architecture (structural shifts like edge computing and caching). Network management has an outsized role in all four areas, requiring automation, fast control loops, and integration into data and control planes.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks help save energy by letting people work from home and control buildings remotely. But the networks themselves use lots of power. This document asks how to make networking technology itself use less power and emit fewer greenhouse gases.

sections.title: Equipment Innovations and Visibility
sections.content:
The most obvious opportunities exist at the equipment level. Hardware and manufacturing improvements can reduce energy consumption and environmental impact: more efficient transmission technology (wireless antennas, optical lasers), reduced heat dissipation, sustainable material sourcing, and recycling. Software-Defined Networking and virtualization enable support for new features through software updates rather than hardware replacement, extending equipment lifetime and reducing embedded carbon costs.

Visibility and instrumentation are prerequisites for optimization. Equipment must provide granular measurement of power consumption at device, line-card, and port levels. Current standardized YANG data models for network energy consumption are lacking. As of 2024, efforts were underway to define green networking metrics and YANG models for power measurement. Equipment should expose energy efficiency ratings and support virtualization scenarios where power consumption attribution is complex.

Beyond monitoring, control knobs for energy-saving policies are needed: power-saving modes common in endpoints but rare in networking equipment, dynamic port down-speeding, and automated threshold-based resource management. The RFC emphasizes that certification and compliance methods must ensure green instrumentation cannot be manipulated to give false data.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things help here: making equipment use less power, and giving network managers detailed visibility into how much power each part uses so they can optimize.

sections.title: Protocol Design for Energy Efficiency
sections.content:
Protocols have multiple opportunities for improvement. Protocol enablers for carbon optimization include discovery mechanisms that handle frequent topology changes from power cycling, fast convergence onto energy-efficient paths without requiring full network reconvergence, and extensions to existing protocols (IGP, BGP) to advertise energy or carbon parameters. Time-Variant Routing work can be leveraged for networks that regularly turn links on and off based on demand.

Protocol optimization concerns traffic transmission rates chosen to maximize energy efficiency. Traffic engineering can minimize flow completion time (FCT) to enable rapid transition to low-power modes. Rate adaptation triggered by intentional congestion can reduce overall traffic; alternatively, protocols can bulk transmission into short high-rate periods rather than spreading it over longer intervals.

Data volume reduction through protocols is critical. Avoiding unnecessary retransmissions, reducing header tax (e.g., through header compression like ROHC), and lowering protocol verbosity all reduce energy consumption. Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) avoids the waste of dropped packets. Protocols should minimize chattiness that prevents equipment from entering sleep mode, avoiding dependence on frequent periodic updates or heartbeats.

Network addressing impacts energy through memory and state requirements. Address tables and forwarding tables can be large, consuming significant memory and power. Geographic routing approaches could be more energy-efficient than Longest Prefix Match lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols can be designed to send less data, avoid waste, and let equipment sleep. For example, sending data in one fast burst instead of slowly over time uses less power.

sections.title: Network-Wide Optimization and Management
sections.content:
The greatest energy-saving opportunities exist at the network level. Network optimization treats carbon footprint as a cost metric to minimize, similar to existing optimization for cost and utilization. This includes carbon-aware traffic steering and routing, placing virtualized functions to minimize energy, and applying machine learning to optimize for carbon footprint while managing trade-offs with other operational goals like redundancy and robustness.

Dimensioning and peak shaving are crucial: networks are dimensioned for peak traffic but consume significant energy during non-peak periods. Peak shaving through traffic redistribution across time and geography, combined with accurate traffic forecasting, can yield outsized sustainability gains by reducing the equipment that must remain powered.

Instrumentation at the network level must associate carbon footprint not just with devices but with concepts meaningful at network scale: flows and paths. Tools must assess and predict carbon intensity of paths, account for carbon footprint of individual flows, and enable green billing schemes that charge users for carbon-equivalent emissions of their communication.

Convergence challenges arise from much greater network dynamicity as resources are continually taken offline and brought back online. Mechanisms must minimize convergence scope (local rather than network-wide), limit state churn, and support prediction and inference to reduce frequency of full recalculation.
sections.plainLanguage: The network level is where the biggest wins happen: routing traffic efficiently, turning equipment off when not needed, and predicting demand so you can power things up only when needed.

sections.title: Architectural Approaches to Green Networking
sections.content:
Architectural shifts offer opportunities beyond incremental improvements. Content Delivery Networks exemplify successful architectural change: retrieving content from local caches is far more energy-efficient than always fetching from distant data centers, saving both network energy and WAN bandwidth. Further savings could come from in-network caching at even greater scale.

Information-Centric Networking approaches propose shifting caching and naming into the network itself, though this increases power demands on network equipment due to larger memory and name lookup hardware requirements. The trade-off between storage-based caching and traditional forwarding is deployment-specific.

Fog computing and edge placement reduce the energy spent on long-distance transmission, but introduce trade-offs: edge processing may be less efficient than large-scale data center computation with high resource multiplexing. Green metrics should account for the full picture, comparing end-to-end energy including transmission and computation.

The RFC emphasizes that networks enable applications in other domains to reduce energy (smart buildings, IoT agriculture). Sustainability is not binary but involves life-cycle thinking: manufacturing, deployment, operations, and end-of-life impacts. Design decisions that avoid hardware replacement may be preferable to incremental efficiency gains requiring new equipment.
sections.plainLanguage: Big changes to how networks are built can save lots of energy. For example, caching content locally is much greener than always fetching from far away.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Security implications arise from greater energy awareness. Adversaries could attempt to disable resources by triggering resource-weaning schemes, or waste energy through attacks that require bringing additional equipment online. New security attack surfaces emerge from exposing energy metrics and carbon parameters through protocols.

Implementation requires careful attention to trade-offs. Energy optimization can conflict with established operational goals like redundancy and load balancing for resilience. Different network domains have different energy challenges: core networks with fluid, multiplexed traffic benefit from optimization at longer timescales, while access networks with bursty traffic require faster adaptation. Any green networking approach must accommodate these differences without destabilizing the network.

The RFC concludes that sustainability is becoming a business necessity for network operators, particularly in data center environments where energy procurement is a growth bottleneck. Telefónica's example shows that year-on-year efficiency gains exceeding 90% since 2015 are achievable, though partly offset by growing data volume. The path forward requires innovation in management practices, control systems, and protocols to maximize energy savings while maintaining network utility and reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: Making networks more efficient can introduce new security risks if not done carefully. Attackers could exploit energy-saving features. And you have to be careful not to break redundancy and backup systems that keep networks reliable.
